subject: Accounting
title: Wirecard: Europe's Biggest Fraud
description: A micro-lesson that makes Wirecard: Europe's Biggest Fraud usable.

hook.text: German fintech darling Wirecard claimed $2.1 billion in bank accounts. The money didn't exist.

buildup.text: Wirecard was a payments processor valued at $28 billion—bigger than Deutsche Bank at its peak.

discovery.text: Journalists at the Financial Times spent years investigating suspicious transactions in Asia.

twist.text: When auditors finally demanded proof of the cash, the banks in the Philippines said the accounts were forged.

climax.text: The CEO was arrested. The COO vanished. Germany's financial regulator faced massive criticism.

punchline.text: Billions in cash that nobody verified. Trust but verify.

quiz.question: What was the key discovery that exposed Wirecard?
options: Banks confirmed the claimed accounts were forged
A routine tax audit found discrepancies

details.summary: Wirecard, a German payment processor, fabricated €1.9 billion in bank balances and inflated revenue for years while regulators protected the company instead of investigating it. This topic examines the forensic red flags, the stunning regulatory failure, and the investigation aftermath.
details.whyItMatters: Wirecard is a masterclass in how institutional failures—regulators attacking journalists instead of investigating—can allow fraud to persist for years even when evidence is publicly available.
takeaways: Wirecard claimed €1.9 billion in escrow accounts at Philippine banks—the money didn't exist
The Financial Times published evidence of fraud for years; Germany's BaFin investigated the journalists instead
COO Jan Marsalek disappeared and is believed to have fled to Russia with help from intelligence contacts

faq.question: What forensic red flags existed at Wirecard?
faq.answer: Red flags included revenue and profit vastly exceeding industry peers, operations concentrated in opaque third-party partners in developing markets, resistance to audit scrutiny of Asian operations, and profit margins that made no economic sense for a payment processor.

faq.question: How did the Wirecard investigation unfold?
faq.answer: The Financial Times published investigative reports starting in 2015. BaFin responded by banning short-selling and filing criminal complaints against reporters. In 2020, EY auditors finally confirmed the €1.9 billion was missing. CEO Markus Braun was arrested; COO Marsalek became a fugitive.
